w: At 4,807 m, this is the highest summit in Europe outside the Caucasus, straddling the disputed France-Italy border. Courmayeur is one of three towns ringing its base, alongside Chamonix and Saint-Gervais-les-Bains. A cable car crosses the range to Chamonix via the Col du Geant.
s: Europe's highest peak, claimed by three valleys
_facts: 4,807.3m; highest in Europe outside the Caucasus
Courmayeur is one of three towns encircling the massif
Cable car crosses to Chamonix via the Col du Geant
11.6km road tunnel beneath the mountain, opened 1965

w: Its highest point, Pointe Walker, reaches 4,208 m and was first climbed on 30 June 1868 by Horace Walker with guides Melchior Anderegg, Johann Jaun and Julien Grange. The lower Pointe Whymper (4,184 m) fell three years earlier, in 1865, to Edward Whymper's party.
s: 4,208m wall first topped by an Englishman's guided party
_facts: 4,208m at Pointe Walker, its highest point
First climbed 30 June 1868 by Horace Walker with guides Anderegg, Jaun and Grange
Pointe Whymper (4,184m) first climbed 1865 by Edward Whymper's party

w: Standing 4,122 m tall in the Mont Blanc massif, its French name is usually translated as 'Green Needle', though some scholars argue the root 'verte' is pre-Celtic for 'high place', making it the High Needle instead. It ranks among the massif's defining spires.
s: The 'Green Needle' that may really mean 'High Needle'
_facts: Name usually read as 'Green Needle'
Possible pre-Celtic origin meaning 'high place'

w: Its French name means 'Cursed Mountain', and until the late 18th century the curse covered its giant neighbour too: Mont Blanc and its satellite summits were collectively called the Montagne Maudite. The peak rises 4,465 m on the Italy-France frontier.
_facts: Name means 'Cursed Mountain'
Mont Blanc itself was once grouped under the name 'Montagne Maudite'

w: At 4,052 m on Mont Blanc's western flank, this has been called one of the range's most attractive satellite peaks. Its south and east ridges form the France-Italy frontier, and the summit is a knife-edge crest of snow and ice: a splendid, serious climb by any route.
s: A knife-edge of snow on Mont Blanc's western flank
_facts: 4,052m, on Mont Blanc's western side
South and east ridges form the France-Italy border
Summit is a knife-edge crest of snow and ice

w: Bolted below the Bosses Ridge at 4,362 m, this unheated duralumin box was meant only as an emergency shelter, never as a base for the ascent, and was built to sleep just 12 people. In practice it has often held considerably more, as storm-bound climbers crowd in wherever they can.
s: An unheated survival box at 4,362m, built for 12
_facts: 4,362m altitude, below the Bosses Ridge on Mont Blanc
An unheated duralumin emergency shelter, not a climbing base
Designed for 12 people, often holds more

a: above Val Veny, Mont Blanc massif
w: This 3,792 m summit sits 3.5 km northeast of Mont Blanc, part of the frontier ridge continuing Mont Maudit's Brenva spur between France and Italy. Easily accessible, it offers a fine viewpoint over the Brenva face and doubles as a popular introduction to alpine climbing at every grade.
s: A beginner's alpine peak with a grandstand Mont Blanc view
_facts: 3,792m, 3.5km northeast of Mont Blanc
Part of the France-Italy frontier ridge
Popular beginner route; also has a north face climb
Viewpoint over the Brenva face and Mont Blanc's south side

w: The 'Black Needle' rises 3,773 m along the Peuterey ridge toward Mont Blanc's summit. Its south ridge route was first climbed by Karl Brendel and Hermann Schaller in 1930; the complete Peuterey ridge traverse followed in 1934. On 21 August 2010, Belgian climber Chloe Graftiaux, 23, fell to her death here.
s: The 'Black Needle', and its ridge's 1934 full traverse
_facts: 3,773m, on the Peuterey ridge toward Mont Blanc
South ridge route first climbed 1930 by Brendel and Schaller
Full Peuterey ridge traverse completed 1934
Belgian climber Chloe Graftiaux died here in 2010

w: Five rock spires over 4,000 m crown the Devil's Ridge on Mont Blanc du Tacul: L'Isolee, Pointe Carmen, Pointe Mediane, Pointe Chaubert and Corne du Diable. Pointe Carmen fell first, in 1923; the rest followed in 1925, to climbers guided by Armand Charlet among others.
s: Five needles climbed one by one, 1923-1928
_facts: Five needles over 4,000m on the Devil's Ridge
First needle climbed 1923, remaining four in 1925
All five crossed in one 1928 expedition by O'Brien, Underhill and guide Armand Charlet

w: At 4,001 m, this peak sits on the Rochefort arete between the Dent du Geant and the Grandes Jorasses, usually taken during a full traverse of that ridge rather than climbed alone. James Eccles reached the summit with guides Alphonse and Michel Payot on 14 August 1873.
s: A 4,001m ridge point first climbed in 1873
_facts: 4,001m, on the Rochefort arete
Between the Dent du Geant and Grandes Jorasses
First climbed 14 Aug 1873 by James Eccles with guides Alphonse and Michel Payot

w: This 3,870 m peak sits on a long France-Italy border ridge that also carries Mont Dolent and the Grandes Jorasses. It rises above the Argentiere Glacier and is usually climbed from that side, setting out from Chamonix; its north face is rated one of the classic ice climbs of the Alps.
s: A classic ice climb above the Argentiere Glacier
_facts: 3,870m, on the France-Italy border ridge
Rises above the Argentiere Glacier
Usually climbed from the Chamonix side
North face rated a classic Alpine ice climb

a: south end of the Mont Blanc massif
w: Four tops make up this mountain at the southern end of the Mont Blanc massif; its highest, the southeast pinnacle, reaches 3,930 m and lies in Italy, while only the northwest top sits on the French border. It forms a chain with the Domes de Miage, above a nature reserve.
s: A four-summited ridge above a nature reserve
_facts: Four summits; highest (southeast) is 3,930m, in Italy
Only the northwest top is on the France-Italy border
Forms a chain with the Domes de Miage
Western slope lies within the Contamines-Montjoie Nature Reserve

w: This ski jumping hill was built for the 1924 Winter Olympics at Chamonix, the first Winter Games ever held. It stood at Le Mont as one of the venues that put the fledgling Winter Olympics, and Chamonix itself, on the sporting map.
s: The ski jump built for the first Winter Olympics
_facts: Built for the 1924 Winter Olympics in Chamonix
The 1924 Games were the first Winter Olympics ever held
Located at Le Mont

w: At 3,759 m, this peak sits on the border ridge between Mont Dolent and the Grandes Jorasses, on the edge of Haute-Savoie and the Aosta Valley. It is usually climbed from Val Ferret on the Italian side, and Courmayeur is its nearest town.
s: A 3,759m ridge point climbed from the Italian side
_facts: 3,759m, on the France-Italy border ridge
Sits between Mont Dolent and Grandes Jorasses
Usually climbed from Val Ferret, Italian side
Nearest town: Courmayeur

w: At 4,041 m, this peak sits at the foot of the Innominata ridge to Mont Blanc's summit, in the Aosta Valley. It is named for English mountaineer and geologist James Eccles, who made the first certain ascent in 1877 with guides Alphonse and Michel Payot, during the first ascent of Mont Blanc de Courmayeur.
s: Named for the Englishman who claimed its first sure ascent
_facts: 4,041m, at the foot of the Innominata ridge to Mont Blanc
Named for mountaineer-geologist James Eccles
First certain ascent 1877, with guides Alphonse and Michel Payot
Possibly climbed earlier, 1874, by J.G.A. Marshall's party
